acceptedAnswer.text: Safety depends on the specific peptide, medical history, dosing, sourcing quality, physician oversight, and ongoing monitoring. Peptides should not be purchased through unverified online sources. When used, they should be prescribed carefully, sourced through legitimate pharmacies, and monitored by a qualified provider.

mainEntity.name: Are peptides the same as hormones?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Peptides and hormones are both signaling molecules, but they are not the same thing. Hormones typically have broader systemic effects, while peptides are short chains of amino acids that can signal specific physiologic pathways.

mainEntity.name: Will everyone benefit from peptide therapy?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Peptide therapy is not appropriate for every patient. Whether it makes sense depends on symptoms, goals, labs, medical history, risk profile, and whether there is a clear physiologic reason to consider it.

Some peptide-based therapies are FDA-approved for specific uses. Others may be compounded under physician supervision, while some are restricted or not appropriate for clinical use. Regulatory status, sourcing, and medical oversight matter because not every peptide discussed online is safe, legal, or appropriate for patient care.

mainEntity.name: Can peptide therapy replace hormone therapy or other treatment?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually, no. Peptide therapy should not be used as a shortcut or replacement for proper medical care. In some cases, peptides may be considered as part of a broader plan that includes hormone care, metabolic support, recovery work, nutrition, sleep, inflammation management, or other treatment.

Physician supervision helps ensure the right peptide is selected, the dose is appropriate, the source is legitimate, and the patient response is monitored over time. It also helps identify when peptide therapy is not appropriate or when another issue should be addressed first.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if a peptide source is legitimate?

acceptedAnswer.text: A legitimate peptide source should involve a licensed medical provider, a credentialed compounding pharmacy, clear dosing instructions, quality controls, sterility standards, and transparent documentation. Be cautious with research-grade peptides, direct-to-consumer peptide websites, vague medical-grade claims, or any provider that skips labs and medical history.

mainEntity.name: What labs should be checked before peptide therapy?

acceptedAnswer.text: The right labs depend on the treatment goal, but a deeper evaluation may include hormones, thyroid markers, metabolic markers, fasting insulin, glucose, HbA1c, lipids, inflammatory markers, recovery-related markers, and sometimes growth hormone axis markers such as IGF-1.

mainEntity.name: What changes when peptide therapy is used appropriately?

acceptedAnswer.text: When peptide therapy is appropriate and properly monitored, patients may notice improvements in areas such as recovery, body composition, metabolic regulation, sleep, libido, inflammation, or energy. The exact outcome depends on the peptide used, the reason it was selected, and the underlying physiology.

mainEntity.name: Will I automatically be prescribed peptides?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Peptides are not automatic. RHM evaluates whether peptide therapy makes sense based on symptoms, labs, health history, goals, and risk profile. If peptides are not appropriate, recommendations may focus on hormones, thyroid function, metabolism, sleep, inflammation, nutrition, or recovery first.
